On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[44] ﴿And We did not give them any scriptures which they could study, nor did We send to them before you any warner.﴾

﴿And We did not give them any scriptures which they could study, nor did We send to them before you any warner.﴾ That is: Allah did not send down to the Arabs any Book before the Qur'an, nor did He send to them any prophet before Muhammad (ﷺ). Yet they used to wish for this and say: "If a warner had come to us, or a Book had been sent down to us, we would have been better guided than others." But when Allah bestowed this favour upon them, they denied it, rejected it, and opposed it. Then, glorified is He, threatened them with His saying:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[45] ﴿And those before them denied, and they had not attained one-tenth of what We had given them, yet they denied My messengers. So how was My disapproval?﴾

﴿And those before them denied﴾ i.e., of the earlier nations and the bygone generations, just as these [people] denied. ﴿And they had not attained﴾ i.e., these [people]: ﴿one-tenth of what We had given them﴾ meaning those [earlier peoples], of wealth, expanse of dominion, prosperity, and civilization. ﴿Yet they denied My messengers. So how was My disapproval?﴾ i.e., My punishment, My retribution, and My vengeance.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[46] ﴿Say, "I only advise you of one thing: that you stand before Allah in pairs and individually, and then reflect. Your companion is not afflicted with madness; he is only a warner to you before a severe punishment."﴾

﴿Say, "I only advise you of one thing: that you stand before Allah﴾ i.e., with one attribute; if you do it, you will have attained the truth. He explained it with His saying: ﴿that you stand before Allah in pairs and individually﴾, i.e., standing sincerely for Allah without favoritism (p-4966), nor ostentation, two by two and one by one.

﴿Then reflect﴾, i.e., upon his matter, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and what he brought of guidance, reform, refinement of morals, and elevating the soul from worshipping what is baser than it, such as idols, to worshipping the Originator of the earth and the heavens, following what is best, rejecting blind imitation, and bringing leaders down to the level of those they lead out of desire for brotherhood and equality, along with other excellences of Islam and its well-known distinctive features mentioned in the books written on this subject.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your companion is not afflicted with madness﴾, i.e., insanity. It is a resumed sentence alerting them that the soundness of his intellect which they knew is sufficient to establish the truthfulness of his claim, for he would not dare to undertake the claim of a grave matter and a momentous affair without verifying confident proof, so that he would be disgraced before all witnesses and cast himself into destruction. How much more so, when many miracles have been joined to him?

It has also been permitted that the clause is suspended (mu'allaq) from it, based on the statement of Ibn Malik: that (tafakkara) is suspended by analogy with verbs of the heart. The reference to him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, as "your companion" is to hint that his condition is well-known and famous among them, for he grew up among them known for strength of intellect, gravity of forbearance, and soundness of speech and action. ﴿He is only a warner to you before a severe punishment﴾, and that is the punishment of the Hereafter and its outcome.

Commentary on the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[47–49] ﴿Say: "Whatever reward I have asked of you, it is yours. My reward is only with Allah, and He is over all things Witness."﴾ ﴿Say: "Indeed, my Lord casts the truth; He is the Knower of the unseen."﴾ [Saba': 48] ﴿Say: "The truth has come, and falsehood can neither originate nor restore."﴾ [Saba': 49]

﴿Say: Whatever reward I have asked of you, it is yours﴾ — meaning: whatever reward I have asked of you for the message, it is yours. The intended sense is the outright negation of asking, and the sincere giving of counsel, by way of metaphor (kinayah), because what a questioner asks for is his own; so he attributed it to the one asked, as a metaphor for his not asking at all. Here "mā" is conditional (shartiyyah). It has also been permitted that it be relative (mawsulah), with the meaning of what he asked of them: ﴿Say: I ask of you no reward for it, except that whoever wills may take a path to his Lord﴾ [al-Furqan: 57], and His saying: ﴿Say: I ask of you no reward for it, except love for the near of kin﴾ [al-Shura: 23]. Taking the path to Him, Exalted is He, is their greatest benefit, and his nearness (peace be upon him) is their nearness. It has also been permitted that it be negating. His saying, ﴿it is yours﴾, is the answer to an implied conditional: that is, if I have not asked you, then it is yours: ﴿My reward is only with Allah, and He is over all things Witness.﴾ ﴿Say: Indeed, my Lord casts the truth﴾ [Saba': 48], meaning: He hurls it against falsehood so that it crushes it and destroys it, or He hurls it across the horizons, which is then a promise of the manifestation of Islam and the elevation of the word of truth. ﴿the Knower of the unseen﴾ [Saba': 48]. ﴿Say: The truth has come﴾ [Saba': 49], meaning: it has appeared, and that is Islam and its excellences. ﴿and falsehood can neither originate nor restore﴾ [Saba': 49] is a metaphor for the vanishing of falsehood and the erasure of its trace, taken from the death of a living thing: for as long as it exists, it either originates an act or restores it; when it perishes, it has no origination and no restoration left. Then this usage spread to everything that has gone, even if no trace of it remains, and even if it was something with a soul. It has also been permitted that "mā" be interrogative, governing what follows it, meaning: what thing can it do?

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[50] ﴿Say: "If I go astray, I only go astray to my own loss; and if I am guided, it is by what my Lord reveals to me. Indeed, He is All-Hearing, Ever-Near."﴾

﴿Say: If I go astray﴾, i.e., from the path of truth: ﴿then I only go astray to my own loss﴾, i.e., because the harm of that returns upon me, or upon my own self, not upon others. ﴿And if I am guided, it is by what my Lord reveals to me﴾, i.e., of right guidance and clear truth. ﴿Indeed, He is All-Hearing, Ever-Near﴾.

If it is asked: the correspondence (al-muqabala) with the sentence before it would require saying, "And if I am guided, then I am guided only for it" (p-4968). Why, then, did he turn away from that to what is mentioned? It is said: the correspondence may be in wording and may be in meaning, and what is here is of the second kind. Its explanation is that the self (al-nafs), whatever is upon it is "by it," i.e., whatever is harmful to it and injurious to it is by its cause and from it, since it is the one that commands to evil (al-ammara bi'l-su'). And whatever is beneficial to it, of what benefits it, is by the guidance of its Lord and His granting it success.

This is a general ruling for every mukallaf (person responsible under the law), and the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) was only commanded to attribute this to his own self because the Messenger, when he is included in its generality, together with the loftiness of his position and the soundness of his way, the others are more entitled to it. Ibn al-Athir, the eminent scholar, pointed to this in his book "al-Mathal al-sa'ir" (The Widely Circulated Example).

The Discussion of the Interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying:

[51] ﴿And if you could see when they are seized with terror, but there is no escape, and they are seized from a near place.﴾

﴿And if you could see when they are seized with terror﴾: that is, these deniers at the time of death, or at the Resurrection, or at the manifestation of the Truth and its authority, and their entry under its control. ﴿but there is no escape﴾: for them, by flight or by seeking refuge, since there is no refuge for them and no place of safety. ﴿and they are seized from a near place﴾: that is, from the surface of the earth to its interior when they die, or from the place of standing to the Fire when they are raised, or they are overtaken with ease after the difficulty of doing so.

The discussion of the words of His Exalted saying:

[52] ﴿And they will say, "We believe in it." But how could they reach [it] from a place far away?﴾

﴿And they will say, "We believe in it."﴾ That is, in Muhammad (ﷺ), or in the Qur'an. ﴿But how could they reach [it] from a place far away?﴾ That is, from where could they obtain faith when they have gone far from the place where it is accepted from them? This is because they have passed on to the Hereafter, which is the abode of recompense, not the abode of trial. Or: because they professed faith with their tongues while faith had not entered their hearts. That is, (according to the interpretation of: ﴿when they are seized with terror﴾ [Saba': 51], by the manifestation of the truth to them in their lifetime, from it) al-Zamakhshari said: "Al-tanawush (reaching out) and al-tanawul (taking hold) are kindred, except that al-tanawush is an easy taking of a thing that is near (p-4969). It is said: nashahu yanushuhu, and tanawashahu al-qawm (the people reached for it together). It is also said: tanawashu fi al-harb (they reached for one another in battle), meaning some of them struck at others." And this is a figurative representation of their seeking what cannot be: that their faith would benefit them at that time, as faith benefits the believers in this world. Their condition is depicted as the condition of one who wants to grasp a thing from a far distance (ghalwa), just as another grasps it from the length of a cubit's measure, a grasp that is easy and without effort. End of quotation. That is: in it there is a metaphorical image (isti'ara tamthiliyya); he likened their faith, where it is not accepted, to one who has a thing that can be taken, but when it is a farsakh away from him, he stretches out his hand to grasp it. And his saying:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[53] ﴿And they had already disbelieved in it before, and they hurl (guesses) about the unseen from a far-off place.﴾

﴿And they had already disbelieved in it before﴾ is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), or a conjoined clause (ma'ṭūf), or a resumptive new sentence (mustaʼnaf). The first is closer (to the meaning).

﴿and they hurl (guesses) about the unseen from a far-off place﴾ means: they cast conjectures (yarjumūna bi-l-ẓann), so they speak of things that did not arise from verification, among their false statements, such as their saying: "He is a sorcerer," "He is a poet," "He is a madman," and "We will not be resurrected," and similar things. All of it is hurled from a distant place, with no nearness to its correspondence in any way.

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 34, verse 54:**

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[54] ﴿And a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire, as was done with their counterparts before. Indeed, they were in disquieting doubt.﴾

﴿A barrier will be placed between them and what they desire﴾, i.e., from the benefit of faith on that Day and from being saved from the Fire through it, or from the matter turning in their favour, because ﴿the help of Allah and the victory﴾ had come. ﴿As was done with their counterparts before﴾, i.e., with their likes among the disbelieving nations. ﴿Indeed, they were in disquieting doubt﴾: from (arabahu), meaning he caused him to fall into suspicion and accusation, so the hamza is for transitivity. Or it is from (arāba al-rajul), meaning he became one who has suspicion, and this is figurative (majāz), either by likening doubt to a person, so that it is an implicit and imaginative metaphor (isti'ārah makniyyah wa takhyiliyyah), or as a metaphorical attribution (isnād majāzī), in which what belongs to the one who doubts is attributed to the doubt itself, for emphasis. This was conveyed by al-Shihab.

[p. 4970] Note: In (al-Iklil), Ibn al-Furs said: Some exegetes have argued from this verse that the doubter is a disbeliever, and they refuted by it those who claim that he is not a disbeliever and that Allah does not punish for doubt. End of quote.

And from Qatada: "Beware of doubt and suspicion, for whoever dies upon doubt will be resurrected upon it, and whoever dies upon certainty will be resurrected upon it."

May Allah keep us alive, and resurrect us upon certainty. Indeed, He is the Most Merciful of the merciful, and the Guardian of the believers.
